title: Async JavaScript, Handwritten: Promises, Microtasks & async/await
summary: A dense study-notes series taking you from promise fundamentals and microtask internals through the four combinators, error propagation, async/await mechanics, real-world concurrency patterns, classic mistakes, and async iteration with async generators — ending with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Promise Fundamentals: States, Executor & Core Methods
points: Definition: a Promise is an object representing the eventual completion (value) or failure (reason) of an async operation
Three states: pending -> fulfilled or rejected; 'settled' means no longer pending, and the state is final and immutable
The executor in new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...}) runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, before any .then is attached
resolve(value) fulfills; resolving with a thenable adopts that thenable's eventual state (resolve chains unwrap)
reject(reason) rejects; throwing inside the executor also rejects the promise with the thrown value
promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected): handlers NEVER run synchronously — they are queued as microtasks
.catch(fn) is shorthand for .then(undefined, fn) and handles any upstream rejection
.finally(fn): runs on either outcome, receives no argument, and passes the result or reason through unchanged
Thenables: any object with a .then method is treated promise-like by the machinery
State transitions are one-way: a second resolve() or reject() call is silently ignored
Handler returns: a plain return fulfills the derived promise; returning a promise makes the chain wait for it
Example: promisify a callback API — wrap setTimeout or fs.readFile into a function returning a promise

chapters.title: The Microtask Queue: How Ordering Actually Works
points: Event loop model: run the current macrotask -> drain the ENTIRE microtask queue -> render -> next macrotask
Microtask queue (jobs): promise reactions, queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver, and every await continuation
Macrotasks (tasks): setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events — one per loop tick
Key rule: microtasks queued DURING the drain also run before the next macrotask — the queue empties completely
Classic puzzle: Promise.resolve().then(log) beats setTimeout(log, 0) — promise always prints first
Each .then link is one job: a chain of n thens resolves across n microtask ticks, not all at once
await suspends the function and schedules its continuation exactly like a .then reaction
Cost model: each await adds a microtask hop — deep sequential chains enqueue many jobs
Starvation: endlessly chaining microtasks blocks rendering and starves timers — an anti-pattern
Node extra: the process.nextTick queue runs BEFORE the promise microtask queue
Worked trace: log order for sync code -> promise -> setTimeout -> second promise, walked tick by tick
Practical impact: the browser does not repaint between chained microtasks — use setTimeout or rAF to yield to paint

chapters.title: Chaining: Value Pipelines & Flat Chains
points: Every .then/.catch/.finally returns a NEW promise — the original is never mutated
Value pipeline: whatever a handler returns becomes the input value of the next .then
Returning a promise from a handler: the chain waits for it and adopts its settled value — flattening, not nesting
Anti-pattern: .then(res => res.then(...)) nests chains — prefer returning to keep one flat line
Rejections skip forward past fulfillment handlers to the nearest .catch — like exceptions unwinding a stack
After a .catch handles an error, the chain returns to fulfilled — recovery lets continuation proceed
Throw Errors, not strings or objects: only real Errors carry a .stack for debugging
Readability: callback pyramids vs flat then-chains — one return per step, one catch at the end
.then(fn).catch(h) vs .then(fn, h): the first also catches errors thrown by fn; the second does not
Mixed sync/async steps: the chain normalizes both — a sync return and a returned promise behave identically downstream
Example: fetch -> response.json() -> transform -> render, with a single final .catch covering all stages
Late attachment is safe: a promise remembers its state, so .then added after settling still fires with the stored value

chapters.title: Error Propagation: From throw to catch
points: A rejection travels down the chain until the first rejection handler — unhandled links in between are skipped
A throw inside ANY handler (fulfillment or rejection) rejects the promise that handler's link returns
Unhandled rejection: rejected with no handler attached by end of tick — fires 'unhandledrejection' (browser) / process event (Node, crashes by default)
try/catch in an async function catches rejections from awaited promises — same semantics as .catch
Placement matters: a mid-chain catch = partial recovery for one section; a final catch = handler for the whole chain
.finally never swallows: errors pass through untouched — but a throw inside finally REPLACES the outcome
Branch handling: define custom error classes and check err instanceof inside catch to route to the right recovery
Anti-pattern: .catch(err => {}) silently swallows failures — always at minimum log or rethrow
Wrap-and-rethrow pattern: catch low-level errors, add context, rethrow so upstream layers see a meaningful error
Rejections are values: multiple .catch handlers attached to one rejected promise EACH fire with the same reason
Mixing styles is risky: an async function with internal .then but no .catch leaks a floating rejection that try/catch misses
Example: validate (throw) -> fetch (network reject) -> json() (parse reject) — one final catch receives whichever failed

chapters.title: async/await Mechanics: What Really Happens
points: An async function ALWAYS returns a promise: returned values get wrapped, thrown errors become rejections
await pauses the async function (never the thread) and resumes its continuation as a microtask when the promise settles
await accepts any thenable and unwraps it; awaiting a plain value passes it through with one microtask hop
Under the hood: async/await is generator + promise machinery — transpilers emit .then chains or a state machine
try/catch/finally around await gives synchronous-style error handling for async code
return vs return await inside try: 'return await p' lets catch see p's rejection; bare 'return p' escapes the try block
The start of an async function runs synchronously — everything before the first await executes immediately
await sequentializes: each await waits for the previous one; use Promise.all when calls are independent
Scope rules: await is legal only inside async functions (plus top-level await in ES modules); async arrows/methods behave the same
Async callbacks don't pause the caller: passing an async fn to a sync API leaves the outer function unaware of it
Uncaught throws inside an async function reject its returned promise — the CALLER is responsible for handling
Example: rewrite a 4-step .then chain as async/await — identical control flow, one try/catch instead of one .catch

chapters.title: Promise.all & Promise.allSettled
points: Promise.all(iterable): fulfills with an array of resolved values in INPUT order, regardless of completion order
Fail-fast: the first rejection rejects the whole all() — sibling promises keep running but their results are discarded (no cancellation)
Empty iterable: all([]) fulfills immediately with []
Non-promise entries pass through unchanged into the results array
Use all() when every result is required — e.g. loading a page that needs user + settings + notifications
Core pattern: Promise.all(ids.map(id => fetchUser(id))) — N requests in parallel, one await
Promise.allSettled(iterable): ALWAYS fulfills with [{status:'fulfilled', value} | {status:'rejected', reason}, ...]
allSettled never short-circuits — ideal for best-effort batches where you collect successes and failures together
Pattern: filter by status to partition results, then retry only the rejected entries
Trade-off: all() is simple fail-fast but loses sibling results; allSettled gives full info but you must inspect statuses
Gotcha: all()'s rejection reason is just the first error, with no index — tag errors with their position if you need it
Example: allSettled over 3 mixed outcomes, reading value vs reason from each entry in a loop

chapters.title: Promise.race & Promise.any
points: Promise.race: settles as soon as the FIRST promise settles — winner may be fulfilled OR rejected
Race use case: timeouts — race the work against a timer that rejects (or resolves a sentinel) after N ms
Race pitfall: the losing promise's later rejection is silently ignored — errors can vanish; losers still run to completion
Promise.any: fulfills with the FIRST FULFILLED value, tolerating earlier rejections
Promise.any all-reject case: rejects with AggregateError whose .errors array holds every reason
any vs race: race = first settle (a fast rejection wins); any = first success (rejections are tolerated)
any use case: racing mirrors/CDNs — first working response wins, dead mirrors just reject harmlessly
Edge cases: race([]) stays pending forever; all/allSettled([]) fulfill with []; any([]) rejects with AggregateError
Real timeout pattern: race + AbortController so the losing request is actually cancelled, not just ignored
Cheat row: all = all must fulfill; allSettled = never rejects; race = first settle; any = first fulfill
Index gotcha: all preserves input order, but race/any return a single winning value with no source info — track it yourself
Examples: withTimeout(task, 500) via race, and any([cdn1, cdn2, cdn3]) with an AggregateError fallback

chapters.title: Concurrency Patterns & Trade-offs
points: Sequential awaits in a loop = sum of latencies; Promise.all = max latency — parallelize 10 x 100ms calls: 1000ms vs 100ms
When sequential is correct: rate limits, order-dependent calls, later requests needing earlier results
Worker-pool pattern: spawn k async workers pulling from a shared queue to keep at most k tasks in flight
Simple semaphore: a counter + queue of resolvers — acquire() waits when full, release() wakes the next waiter (p-limit style)
Retry with backoff: loop attempts, exponential delay + jitter, and only retry transient errors (network/5xx), never 4xx
Timeout helper: race against a timer AND abort the underlying work with AbortController — cancel, don't just ignore
Promise.withResolvers() (ES2024): exposes resolve/reject outside the executor — the modern deferred for event bridge code
Fire-and-forget done right: floating promises still need a .catch (or a global unhandledrejection tripwire)
Async memoization: cache the PROMISE, not the value — concurrent callers share one in-flight operation instead of stampeding
Cancellation reality: promises have no built-in cancel — thread an AbortSignal everywhere and check signal.aborted in loops
Trade-off table: parallel (fastest, fail-fast) vs sequential (ordered, gentle on servers) vs pooled (bounded load)
Example: run 100 jobs 5 at a time — chunked Promise.all batches, or a reusable limit(concurrency, tasks) helper

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Debugging
points: forEach(async ...) bug: forEach ignores the returned promise — the loop moves on and rejections escape unhandled; use for...of or map+all
Awaiting inside a loop when calls are independent: accidental serialization — batch with Promise.all instead
Floating promises: calling an async function without await/catch silently drops rejections — enable the no-floating-promises lint rule
try/catch does NOT catch rejections from non-awaited promises inside the same block — a classic false sense of safety
The bare 'return p' in try bug: skips catch because the returned promise rejects outside the try — return await to fix
Promise.all does not cancel losers: after one rejection the other side-effecting requests keep running
Throwing non-Error values: loses .stack and breaks instanceof-based handling — always throw new Error(...) or subclasses
Misplaced catch: putting .catch too early turns later failures into fulfilled recovery values that flow downstream
this-binding: passing obj.method as a callback loses this — bind it or wrap in an arrow function
Debugging: async stack traces are stitched but shallow — label steps, use async_hooks (Node), and log rejections at boundaries
Tripwire: a global unhandledrejection listener turns silent failures into visible errors during development
Bug->fix example: forEach(async item => await save(item)) that 'works locally, fails in prod' — rewritten as for...of with try/catch

chapters.title: Async Iteration & the Big Picture
points: for await...of: iterates async iterables, awaiting each next() — the loop body pauses per item
Protocol: an object with Symbol.asyncIterator returning { next(): Promise<{value, done}> }
Async generators: async function* with yield — each yield may await; consumed naturally with for await
Producer pattern: an async generator yields paginated API pages one by one while the consumer stays a simple loop
Error handling: try/catch around the loop catches a next() rejection; break or return calls the iterator's return() for cleanup
Node streams are async iterables: for await (const chunk of readable) — pull-based, backpressure-friendly consumption
Throughput note: items process strictly one at a time — gather pages (or chunks) into arrays and Promise.all within a chunk for speed
Combinator mismatch: spread and Array.from need sync iteration — collect an async iterable into an array with a loop first
Safe teardown: breaking out of a for-await runs the generator's finally blocks — resources close predictably
Comparison: callback/event streams vs async iterators — pull-based, single consumer, natural backpressure, try/catch friendly
Series recap: the microtask queue explains ALL ordering; combinators are settle strategies; rejections propagate until a handler catches them
Cheat sheet: all = need everything; allSettled = report everything; race = timeout; any = first win; for await = streams & pagination
